who-this-is-for.text: This page is for a reviewer who wants to play a naming claim instead of reading a walkthrough. The first-release naming profile is an explicit, labelled, unaccepted candidate, not the generic registry demo, and no on-chain acceptance is claimed. Open the simulator and choose the m1-naming profile.

what-you-can-do.text: Queue the first claim for the demo spelling alice: the claim waits with an application approval while the key stays absent, because approval reserves nothing. Queue a competing claim for the same spelling; two claims may both sit pending. Fold the first pending claim: the first valid absent-key fold succeeds, alice becomes Active, and the record carries the four certified fixture fields unchanged. Fold the competing claim: it is refused with occupied-key, because uniqueness is decided only when a certified Insert folds. Resolve alice with an authenticated view: the observation is active with the payment destination, control address, next-control commitment, and retirement quorum. Finally submit a crafted Delete: the naming transition parses the generic action shape and refuses it by name with naming-no-delete.

what-you-see-when-it-is-refused.text: Every refusal names its intended condition, and a generic exception is a defect. The table lists the duplicate fold refused with occupied-key, the crafted delete refused with naming-no-delete, the unapproved queue refused with application-approval, the substituted representative refused with representative-identity, the misbound proposal refused with insert-binding, and the unauthenticated view refused with unauthenticated.

how-the-pieces-relate.text: The generic foundation of forty-one proved declarations stays upstream. The naming layer adds fixtures, queueing, folding, and observation with seventeen proved declarations of its own; the m1-naming engine transcribes that layer and never drives Lean from the browser. Choosing the profile is an explicit act: until m1-naming is selected its controls stay inert, and neither engine silently becomes the other.

what-is-proved-and-what-is-checked-here.text: Seventeen naming theorem declarations are proved in Lean from the standard axioms alone, separately from the generic forty-one. Seven record the user-facing claim contract; ten more pin transition, queue-validation, and resolution equations across the public boundary. The simulator replays a Lean-authored naming corpus of thirty-four rows and requires byte-identical verdicts, and the page's self-test replays the same corpus in the browser. Finite checks remain finite: they measure the transcription and prove nothing about acceptance.

fixture-fields-and-finite-model-limits.text: The playable claim card carries four fixture fields: an optional canonical payment destination, a canonical base or enterprise controller address with a payment-key credential, a thirty-two-byte next-control commitment, and a threshold quorum of payment-key hashes. They are finite-model values, not economic policy. Continue to the playable lifecycle for maintenance, recovery, and split retirement. Naming claim cancellation remains on hold and has no button; retirement request withdrawal is a distinct refusal case.

status-of-this-candidate.text: The claim, fold, and resolve naming profile is an unaccepted candidate: proven in Lean, replayed in the simulator, and playable in the browser. The Nix-built documentation archive packages its raw model, corpus, replay inputs, and exact identities for review. Building that bundle is not release publication or on-chain acceptance. The live preview is bound to the pull-request head and states that the candidate is unaccepted.
